1.pericope_label: When thou sittest to eat with a ruler, consider diligently what is before thee: put a knife to thy throat if thou be a man given to appetite: labour not to be rich: for riches certainly make themselves wings, they fly away as an eagle toward heaven

schools.summary: Henry treats the ruler’s table as a lesson in entering temptation, since the guest sees such a table as he has seldom seen and thinks only of the honour done him, forgetting the snare, while the temptation may be stronger to a man not used to such entertainments than to one who always sits down to a good table, and a wise host will take it as an affront for a guest to disorder himself; he says that as some are given to appetite so others are given to covetousness, that men cheat themselves as much by setting their hearts on money as on dainties, and that those who aim at great things make their life a perfect drudgery and a perpetual hurry, so that a man should be master of what he has rather than its slave.

Gill offers three senses for the knife at the throat, a restraint on too much talk at such a table where men grow free after eating and drinking, a mortifying of the appetite like the cutting off of a right hand, or a reminder that the guest sits in danger and that freedom with the food would be as good as cutting his own throat; he allows that the dainties may be lawfully desired but not sinfully lusted after, and takes the labour forbidden to be the over-anxious kind, carried to weariness and to gaping for breath.

Clarke gives the practical version, to eat moderately at the table of one’s betters, not to appear as if half starved at home, and not to eat of unaccustomed delicacies which please without profiting, calling these prudential cautions for anyone who would avoid the conduct of a clown; he quotes the maxim of the world in a Latin line, that a man should get a fortune honestly if he can but if not get one at all events, calls it the devil’s counsel and notes how well it is followed, and warns that a man who gets wealth and forgets the poor will find the curse of God a canker in his gold. Wesley takes the knife for a restraint on appetite, glosses the wisdom to be ceased from as the worldly wisdom that persuades men to use all possible means of getting riches, and says the riches go swiftly, strongly and irrecoverably.

Ellicott corrects the received rendering of the first verse, since the reader is to consider not what is before him but who, the host being no equal but one who if offended might do him deadly harm, and calls the dainties deceitful because an unguarded word in the insecurity of the festive hour could ruin a guest; he glosses the wisdom to be ceased from as cleverness shown in piling up wealth, and would render the fifth verse as an eagle flying toward heaven, far beyond reach. Keil and Delitzsch read the first verse the same way, render the second as a warning to the man of good appetite, and dispute the grammar with several scholars who make the line a statement rather than a command, answering that the tense continues the exhortation and that their reading would have required the words in another order.

debates: What is to be considered at the ruler’s table? Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch both correct the received rendering, making it who is before thee rather than what, since the host is no equal but one who could destroy as easily as favour.

Is the second verse a command or a statement? Keil and Delitzsch dispute the grammar with several scholars who read it as a statement, holding that the tense continues the exhortation and that their reading would have required a different word order.
What is the knife at the throat? Gill gives three senses, a curb on talk, a mortifying of appetite, and a figure of the guest’s own danger; Wesley and Clarke keep the second.
outliers: Clarke quotes a Latin maxim on getting a fortune honestly if one can and at all events if one cannot, and calls it the devil’s counsel, well followed.
Ellicott explains the deceitfulness of the dainties socially rather than physically, as food offered without friendship at a table where a careless word may ruin a guest.
Henry observes that the temptation of such a table is stronger for a man unused to it than for one who always dines well.
themes: who is before thee, not what
a knife held to the appetite
dainties that please without profiting
the drudgery of aiming high
riches on an eagle’s wings

6.pericope_label: Eat thou not the bread of him that hath an evil eye: for as he thinketh in his heart, so is he: speak not in the ears of a fool: remove not the old landmark, and enter not into the fields of the fatherless: for their redeemer is mighty

schools.summary: Henry notices that both classes already warned are exposed here, the man given to appetite and the man who saves at home being alike glad of another man’s table, and describes the host with a fair tongue and an evil eye who grudges his guests every bit, whose feast is his own penance, and who ought not to add the guilt of dissimulation by inviting friends he cannot welcome; he treats the ninth verse as the rule against casting pearls before swine, since some will despise not only a wise man’s words but the wisdom in them, so that a wise man is advised to hold his peace; and he says the fatherless are affronted in their own person and God in his, that his omnipotence is engaged for their protection, and that being children they do not even apprehend the wrong done them.

Gill makes the seventh verse a rule of judgment, that a man is not what his mouth declares him but what his heart thinks, which his looks and actions discover; he says speaking to a fool is beating the air and speaking to the wind; and he takes the morsel to turn in the stomach as soon as the guest understands he is not welcome.

Clarke says shortly that one should never eat with a stingy man, since he grudges every morsel, and that on reflection the guest will blame himself for accepting; and he sets out what the office of the kinsman covered, the right of the next in blood to redeem an alienated estate, to avenge the blood of a murdered relative and to marry a brother’s childless widow, observing that the strength spoken of lies in the justness of the claim, the extent of his influence and the powerful abettors of such a cause, while here, the orphans having no kinsman, God takes up their cause and the heaviest curse of God falls on those who rob an orphan. Wesley judges the grudging host by the constant temper of his mind rather than by his words, and keeps the kinsman as the one to whom it belongs to avenge their wrongs.

Keil and Delitzsch take the seventh verse as a picture of a man reckoning with himself while he says eat and drink, define the evil eye as the envy and selfishness of egoism, and note that the Greek version refers the look to enchantment, the same words in several languages serving for eyeing, bewitching and envying; they explain that speaking in the ears does not mean whispering but speaking so as to be distinctly perceived, and that the fool is the heavy and dull man whose heart is covered as with grease against better knowledge; and they observe that the tenth verse is made new out of parts of two earlier proverbs, giving the verb the sense of unjustly invading another man’s ground. Ellicott calls the host sordid and grudging, one who calculates the cost of every morsel, reads the vomiting as disgust at hospitality not freely offered and the lost sweet words as thanks spent on a cold welcome, and says it is a waste of time to explain matters to a dull man.

debates: What is the evil eye? Keil and Delitzsch make it the envy and selfishness of egoism and note that the Greek version refers the look to enchantment; Ellicott and Clarke keep it to a sordid and grudging temper that counts the cost of every morsel.

Why should a wise man not speak to a fool? Keil and Delitzsch say the dull heart is covered as with grease against better knowledge and has only contempt for what is offered; Henry adds that such men despise the wisdom in the words as well as the words, and advises silence.

Who redeems the fatherless? Clarke sets out the full office of the next of kin and observes that these orphans have none, so that God takes the office himself; Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott say the same, and Wesley keeps the kinsman’s duty of avenging wrongs.
outliers: Henry calls the grudging host’s entertainment his own penance, since he loves his money too much and his friends too little to enjoy what he pays for.
Keil and Delitzsch trace the words for eyeing, bewitching and envying across several languages in explaining the evil eye.
Clarke lists the three duties of the kinsman-redeemer, over the estate, the murdered relative and the childless widow.
themes: a host who counts every morsel
words wasted on a covered heart
the feast that is its own penance
a landmark moved in the dark
the orphan who has no kinsman

12.pericope_label: Apply thine heart unto instruction and thine ears to the words of knowledge: withhold not correction from the child: my son, if thine heart be wise, my heart shall rejoice: let not thine heart envy sinners, but be thou in the fear of the Lord all the day long

schools.summary: Henry reads the twelfth verse as a parent persuading a child to give his mind to his book and his catechism, since the heart is applied to the instruction when the instruction is applied to the heart; he allows that a tender parent can scarcely find in his heart to correct a child but finds it necessary, the stripes being those of the sons of men and not such as we give to beasts, and the rod keeping the child from the courses that would kill him; and he says sinners are to be pitied rather than envied, their prosperity being their portion and indeed their poison, while the fear of the Lord is to be ours as our employment and as our element.

Gill reads the twelfth verse as a call to bring the heart to the place of instruction and not the body only, insists that the stripes be proportioned to the fault and to what the child can bear, explains the reins as the seat of the affections, and takes the promised end for an end both of the prosperity of the wicked and of the afflictions of the righteous, noting that some render the word a reward.

Clarke notes that the correction of children was a favourite point of discipline with this writer, and reads the end promised in the eighteenth verse as another life, the expectation being one of blessed immortality which shall not be cut off, for which he quotes two old English versions. Wesley calls correction a likely way to prevent a child’s destruction and makes the promised end a happy one for those who fear God.

Keil and Delitzsch observe that the twelfth verse may be taken as offering discipline or as applying the heart to it, according as the divine origin or the human medium is accented; they settle the promise of the thirteenth, which does not say the child will not fall under destruction nor that the blow must not be one he dies of but that he will not die of it, and take the emphatic pronoun following to mean that the man who corrects is the man who saves; they note that wisdom is inborn in no one and support it with an Arab proverb, adding its second half in a note and recording where they heard it; and they object to the versions that make the second half of the seventeenth verse an independent clause, since one may speak of acting or walking in the fear of God but not of being in it. Ellicott says a moderate correction will not injure a child but quite the reverse, reads the deliverance from hell as deliverance from the abode of the dead, explains the reins as the seat of the deepest affections, and makes the promised end one that shall be peace.

debates: What does it mean that the child shall not die? Keil and Delitzsch reject both the sense that he will not fall under destruction and the sense that the blow must not be fatal, and settle on the plain assurance that he will not die of the correction; Ellicott and Wesley agree that moderate correction will not injure him.

Should the second half of the seventeenth verse stand alone? Several versions make it an independent clause, be thou daily in the fear of the Lord; Keil and Delitzsch object that one may act or walk in the fear of God but not be in it.

What is the end promised in the eighteenth verse? Clarke reads it as another life and a blessed immortality, Ellicott as an end that shall be peace, Gill as an end both to the prosperity of the wicked and to the afflictions of the righteous.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch quote an Arab proverb that the wise man knows how the fool feels because he was once a fool, and add in a note the second half of it together with the name of the missionary from whom they heard it.
Henry reports a reading by which the seventeenth verse forbids not envying sinners but imitating them.
Clarke supports his reading of the promised end by quoting two old English versions.
themes: the heart brought to the place of instruction
a rod that will not kill
wisdom inborn in no one
envy or imitation of sinners
an end that is not yet come

19.pericope_label: Hear thou, my son, and be wise, and guide thine heart in the way: be not among winebibbers: hearken unto thy father that begat thee, and despise not thy mother when she is old: buy the truth, and sell it not: the father of the righteous shall greatly rejoice

schools.summary: Henry takes the passage as advice for parents to give their children, holding that hearing is at once evidence of wisdom and the means of more, since wisdom comes by hearing as faith does; that we owe reverence to the fathers of our flesh who were the instruments of our being and much more to the Father of our spirits; and that when the mother is grown old the children are commonly grown up but are not therefore past being taught.

Gill notes that hearing is the road to being wise unto salvation, allows that wine may be drunk with moderation but not in the company of excessive drinkers, and adds that a father who has lived longer has the larger experience; he denies that buying the truth means buying books, as one rabbi understood it, since the Bible should indeed be bought but that does not reach the sense; and on the joy of a righteous man’s father he restricts the rejoicing to a son who is righteous rather than rich and to a father who is himself righteous, since wicked men are unconcerned about a son’s character so long as he thrives.

Clarke surveys the chapter and observes how much of it is given to eating and drinking, the pupil being directed on his conduct at the tables of the rich, on his dealings with the covetous, and on public entertainments where riot and debauch were usual, and he borrows from Calmet four reasons for the warnings, the useless expense, the loss of time, the danger of bad company, and the danger of contracting irregular habits; he calls the caution against despising an old mother very necessary, since very old women are generally helpless and burdensome, while holding that this does not lessen the child’s duty; and he says the knowledge of God is to be acquired at all events and guarded even at the risk of life, quoting an old English version. Wesley expands the guiding of the heart as ordering the whole course of one’s affections and actions, and would purchase the truth on any terms.

Keil and Delitzsch render the last line of the twenty-first verse as sleepiness clothing a man in rags; they consider how this part of the book is put together, since the verses about the father and mother can be read as independent couplets while the last leans back on the first, so that the four form a whole and the compiler may have found two of them already made; and they call the verses following a hexastich warning against unchastity, in which what earlier chapters set out at length is repeated in miniature pictures. Ellicott renders the opening as a charge to hear whatever others may do, takes the way for the way of God, glosses the drowsiness as what follows such debauches, and describes the truth of the twenty-third verse under three heads, wisdom and self-discipline and understanding, all to be had from God without money and without price.

debates: How is this part of the book put together? Keil and Delitzsch judge that the four verses on father and mother form a whole, since the last leans back on the first, and suggest that the compiler found two of them already made and gave the others their present form.

What is bought when truth is bought? Ellicott describes it under three heads, wisdom and self-discipline and understanding, all given by God without price; Gill denies that books are meant, though the Bible should be bought; Clarke and Wesley make it a purchase at any cost.
Whose joy is promised in the twenty-fourth verse? Gill restricts it to a father who is himself righteous, since wicked men are unconcerned about a son’s character so long as he thrives in the world.
outliers: Clarke borrows from Calmet four reasons for the chapter’s warnings about entertainments, the expense, the loss of time, the bad company and the risk of irregular habits.
Clarke calls the caution against despising an aged mother very necessary because very old women are generally helpless and burdensome, and holds that this makes no difference to the duty owed them.
Gill reads the twenty-fifth verse as a wish rather than a promise, that a child should make his parents’ old age easy by ministering to their necessities and following their example.
themes: hearing as the road to wisdom
a chapter much occupied with the table
four verses that form one whole
truth bought at any price
a father who rejoices in righteousness

26.pericope_label: My son, give me thine heart, and let thine eyes observe my ways: for a whore is a deep ditch, and a strange woman is a narrow pit: she also lieth in wait as for a prey, and increaseth the transgressors among men: who hath woe? who hath sorrow?

schools.summary: Henry treats the passage as fair warning against drunkenness and adds the counsel that goes with it, that red wine was accounted the best and is called the blood of the grape, and that some wine looks so well it seems to say come and drink me, moving itself aright and going down smoothly; but a man is to be ruled by reason and religion rather than by sense, and must not let the heart walk after the eye, which is a deceitful guide, since those who would be kept from any sin must keep from all its occasions and beginnings.

Gill says the request for the heart is not a man’s word to his son, since the claim to a heart belongs to God and not to a creature, and makes it the word of Wisdom to his own, the meaning being to give the heart neither to women nor to wine but to him who asks it; he takes the deep ditch for insatiable appetite, collects two classical comparisons, one likening such a woman to the sea which devours whatever you give it and another naming her after the whirlpool that swallows all a man has, and adds that the ditch has no bottom, so that those who fall keep sinking till they reach the bottomless pit; and on her lying in wait he reports an interpreter who reads a man of prey and prefers himself a beast of prey, ravenous and never satisfied.

Clarke makes the request for the heart the speech of God to every human soul and reduces the exhortation to three words, believe, love and obey, which he calls the sum of God’s counsels to every child of man; he states that more iniquity springs from this one source than from any other cause in the whole system of sin, and that women and strong drink cause many millions to transgress; and he reads the opening questions of the drinking poem physiologically, taking the first two interjections not as words but as the natural sounds men make in drink, with the contentions over subjects the drinkers cannot discuss, the wounds from falling out about nothing, and the red eyes either bloodshot with drink or blackened in a fight.

Keil and Delitzsch mark the transition from uncleanness to drunkenness and account for it, since the two sins are nearly related, drunkenness exciting fleshly lust, and a man made in the image of God must first brutalize himself with drink before he can wallow with delight in the mire of sensuality; they note that the poem which follows outgrows the couplet form of the rest and becomes an ode, and render its opening as a string of questions. Ellicott observes that the heart is the one gift worthy of acceptance that man can offer and the only one God will accept, yet the very offering a man tries to keep back, putting alms and unreal prayers and outward observances in its place; he calls the vice of the twenty-eighth verse a fruitful source of faithlessness towards man and God alike, glosses the wounds as those that might have been avoided, and would render the last question as dimness rather than redness of eyes.

debates: Who asks for the heart in the twenty-sixth verse? Gill denies it can be a father speaking, since the claim to a heart belongs to God alone, and makes it the word of Wisdom; Clarke makes it the speech of God to every human soul; Ellicott treats it as the one offering God will accept.

Why does the chapter pass from unchastity to drink? Keil and Delitzsch say the sins are nearly related, since drunkenness excites fleshly lust and a man must first brutalize himself before he can take delight in sensuality.
What are the woe and the sorrow of the twenty-ninth verse? Clarke takes them not as words but as the natural sounds of men in drink, and reads the whole list as the physical marks of the drinker.
outliers: Gill collects two classical comparisons for the strange woman, one to the sea that devours all it is given and one to the whirlpool that swallows a man’s substance.
Clarke reduces the whole exhortation of the twenty-sixth verse to three words, believe, love and obey.
Keil and Delitzsch observe that the drinking poem outgrows the couplet form of the surrounding proverbs and becomes an ode.
themes: a heart claimed by its maker
a ditch without a bottom
the two sins that keep company
sounds that pass for words
wine that invites the eye

30.pericope_label: They that tarry long at the wine, they that go to seek mixed wine: look not thou upon the wine when it is red: at the last it biteth like a serpent and stingeth like an adder: thine eyes shall behold strange women: they have stricken me and I was not sick

schools.summary: Gill describes the men who will not stir from the wine and spend whole days and nights over it; he would render the thirty-first verse because it is red, notes that red was the most esteemed colour there, and allows a man to look at the colour and judge the goodness of a wine while forbidding the greedy eye that raises a vehement desire; he lists the consequences of the sting, nausea and giddiness of head, weakness of the eyes, trembling in the limbs, palsy and gout, with sharp reflections in an awakened conscience; and he gives both senses of the strange things, other men’s wives or the strange sights a drunken man fancies, seeing double and imagining that trees walk.

Clarke makes the warning personal, since however good and pure the wine may be it will be a snare to a man addicted to it who has no self-command; he answers the thirty-third verse with six lines of Herbert on the drunkard who has lost the reins and is outlawed by himself; he draws out the picture of a man who climbs the shrouds while drunk, clasps the mast-head and falls asleep, from which he must fall either to the deck or into the sea, and turns to the reader with the chapter’s own figure of a knife at the throat; and he closes by observing that after all this abuse the man proposes to repeat it, since sin makes a man contemptible in life, miserable in death and wretched for ever. Wesley gives both senses of mixed wine, says the wine seems to smile upon a man, and reports the drunkard needing only sleep before returning to his course.

Ellicott takes the verb of the thirtieth verse for testing wine to see whether it suits the drinker, and notes that ancient wines were not generally drunk pure but diluted or spiced; he renders the clauses of the thirty-first verse as sparkling and as gliding easily down the throat, gives both senses for the strange things of the thirty-third, impurity as the constant attendant of drunkenness or the fantastic visions of a disordered brain, and offers for the thirty-fourth both the sleeper drowned by trusting a glassy surface and the man hurled from the mast by every roll of the ship, adding that the verse may mean the ground itself seems to rock. Keil and Delitzsch ask whether the words for its end are the subject of the thirty-second verse, as two old versions and one scholar take them, and answer that the end of the wine is not like a serpent but like the bite of one, the wine itself being what is like the serpent, so that the clause reads: its end is, like a serpent it biteth.

debates: Are the words for its end the subject of the thirty-second verse? Keil and Delitzsch report two old versions and a scholar who take them so and make the verbs attributive, and answer that the end of the wine is not like a serpent but like the bite of one.

Does the drunkard see strange women or strange things? Gill and Ellicott both give the two senses, the one taking in other men’s wives and the excess that leads to whoredom, the other the fantastic visions of a disordered brain.

What does the sleeper in the sea illustrate? Ellicott offers the man drowned for trusting a glassy surface, the man hurled from the masthead by a roll of the ship, and the drunkard for whom the ground itself seems to rock.
outliers: Clarke quotes six lines of Herbert on the drunkard who forfeits his manhood, and elsewhere pictures a drunken man asleep at the mast-head with the deck or the sea beneath him.
Ellicott explains that ancient wines were not generally drunk pure but diluted with water or flavoured with spices.
Gill distinguishes the lawful looking that judges a wine by its colour from the greedy eye that raises a vehement desire.
themes: wine tested before it is drunk
a colour that must not be coveted
the wine itself, not its end, the serpent
strange women or strange sights
asleep at the mast-head
